alisa: Quick sync — I ran a side-by-side of the KV prefix cache with the same model binary but different traffic: our replay harness vs the synthetic generator. Replay shows 6.3% lower overall prefix hitrate and a 12% higher p95 latency for small sequences. Not sure if it's replay fidelity, arrival jitter, or batching heuristics hitting different kernels.
ben: Noted. Did you preserve arrival times and client-side batching behavior in the replay? Small timing differences can push requests into different batching windows and flip kernel selection.
alisa: Yes, --preserve-arrival was on. I also forced identical seed for the synthetic generator. Still diverged.
dmitri: Can you paste the harness commands and the top-level profiler output? Need to check if we hit different kernels (mini-kernel vs fused) or different batch-size distributions.
alisa: Sure — runs below:
```
# replay
./replay_harness --trace=prod_trace.2026-10.bin --rate=5000 --seed=42 --preserve-arrival --kv-mode=prefix --record-kv-stats

# synthetic
./synthetic_gen --dist=seqlen_hist.json --rps=5000 --seed=42 --kv-mode=prefix --record-kv-stats
```
perf-bot: smoke results uploaded: s3://redwood-ci/perf/replay-vs-synth/1934567890/summary.log
perf-bot: key metrics: replay.hit=0.713, synth.hit=0.776, replay.p95=38ms, synth.p95=33ms, replay.avg-kernel-time=2.8ms, synth.avg-kernel-time=2.4ms
kiley: Two quick suspects: 1) distribution of prefix reuse across distinct keys (hot tail) — replay has more long-tail unique prefixes which hurts warmup; 2) inter-arrival micro-jitter causing smaller effective batch sizes so different kernel paths.
ben: Also check eviction churn during warmup. If replay replay-steps cause more rapid unique key arrivals, cache thrashing will hide hot prefixes and degrade hitrate. Did you compare eviction counts and orphan evictions?
alisa: I grabbed kv stats; excerpt:
```
# from instrumented runtime
total_ops: 1_200_000
cache_hits: 855_600
cache_misses: 344_400
evictions: 52_300
orphan_evictions: 8_900
prefetches_issued: 120_000
```
Note: synthetic run had evictions: 30_200, orphan_evictions: 2_100
dmitri: That's a huge delta in orphan evictions. That suggests concurrency races in our eviction path are triggered more by the replay pattern. We should reproduce with a single-threaded worker to rule out correctness vs race conditions.
kiley: Agreed. Also record kernel selection histogram (batch-size -> kernel name). We want to know how many calls went through small-batch kernels vs fused-kernel.
alisa: I added that and here is the kernel histogram (replay vs synth):
```
# format: kernel_name: count
replay: small-kernel: 710_000, fused-kernel: 320_000
synth:  small-kernel: 490_000, fused-kernel: 440_000
```
ben: So replay biases toward small kernels — explains the slower per-token kernel time and lower batching efficiency. Why is replay producing smaller batches? Check arrival clustering, and whether the replay harness replays client think times that break batching windows.
dmitri: For apples-to-apples (side-by-side) comparisons, we should lock down these variables: same arrival timestamps, same client-side think times, identical concurrency (number of client threads), and a deterministic kernel-selection policy toggle so we can force the same kernel path for both runs.
kiley: Suggestion for methodology doc (short):
- Phase 0: deterministic seed + freeze model binary + record all runtime flags
- Phase 1: Replay with --preserve-arrival and synthetic with generated arrivals copied from replay (i.e., synth uses the exact timestamp stream) so arrival jitter is identical
- Phase 2: Repeat with concurrency=1 to validate functional correctness and eviction semantics
- Phase 3: Enable full concurrency and compare kernel-histogram, eviction counters, batch-size distribution, and per-kernel latencies
- Phase 4: If differences persist, enable per-request tracing for a tiny sample (1000 requests) and inspect KV warmup sequences
ben: Add: normalize for warmup policy — either both runs start with empty cache or both start from a recorded checkpoint. Don't mix one prewarmed and one cold.
alisa: Implemented Phase 1 already by copying timestamps into synthetic generator — that narrowed hitrate gap to 1.2% and p95 difference to 2ms. So arrival pattern was a large factor.
dmitri: Good. The remaining delta could be due to subtle client headers or routing that changes prefix hashing and therefore key placement. Are we certain both runs used identical prefix normalization? (case, trimming)
kiley: Also check the replay harness' transport emulation. If it uses different TCP buffering, the runtime may read different-sized chunks and affect parsing/queueing.
alisa: Action items:
- ben: add kernel-selection histogram to the runtime debug dump (per-bench-run)
- dmitri: run single-threaded replay vs synth and attach full eviction trace (include stack traces if possible)
- kiley: add small sampled per-request trace capture (1000 reqs) with kv op timeline for Phase 4
- alisa: produce a short methodology doc and CI job to run the side-by-side sequence nightly
ben: I'll push a PR to expose kernel histograms and batch-size distributions to the summary collector.
perf-bot: job queued: perf/compare/1934567890 — will run nightly with current artifacts and upload artifacts to s3
alisa: Thanks team. Once we have deterministic harness runs and kernel histograms we can move to tune batching heuristics without chasing harness artifacts.
ben: One more note — when you tune batching heuristics, put a guard: do not switch default kernel selection until we have a regression test that runs the recorded timestamp stream and checks hitrate delta < 0.5%.
alisa: Agreed. I'll draft the regression test spec and post it here for review.
kiley: LGTM. Small/realistic sample traces are the key to debugging the eviction race vs warmup behavior.
